Manu ( 611 ) Ch. 5

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** When there is an extremely intense craving for eating meat, one should curb that desire by using this method, rather than committing animal slaughter. He says "one should make." A ghee-animal is a product of ghee, being an animal in form equal to animal flesh; likewise, a flour-animal. <term>Saṅge</term> <gloss>in intense desire</gloss>. Some say it means "overpowering by ghosts," but because that is not well-known in the world, the meaning is simply intense attachment. 37.

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** <term>Saṅga</term> <gloss>attachment</gloss>: due to a craving for eating meat, one should create an animal replica made of ghee or flour and eat that, but one should never wish to kill animals without the specific purpose of a sacrifice to the deities. 37.

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** "Ghee-animal" means an animal replica made of ghee. <term>Saṅge</term> means in the state of being attached to animal sacrifice, or when there is a craving for food. This applies to required <term>smārta</term> <gloss>traditional law</gloss> rites, but not to Vedic rites, because in the latter, the omission of the eleven <term>paśu</term> <gloss>sacrificial animal</gloss> offerings would be a fault. Therefore, it is said that slaughter in a sacrifice is not slaughter. 37.

( 5 ) **Nandana:** He says "one should make" to indicate that one should not commit violence in the prescribed manner. In the case of <term>saṅge</term> <gloss>in an assembly/festival</gloss>—that is, when there is a gathering of relatives and others—one should offer a ghee-animal. Instead of an animal, one should provide abundant ghee, or flour cakes, and the like. 37.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** One should prepare a ghee-animal when there is attachment. One should do the same with a flour-animal. One should never wish to kill an animal in vain. 37.

### As many as are the hairs on the animal, so many times does the slayer of an animal in vain suffer death in birth after birth in the hereafter. 38.

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** He suffers death as many times as there are hairs in each of his births. The "slayer of an animal in vain" is one who performs animal slaughter not enjoined by <term>śruti</term> <gloss>Vedic revelation</gloss> or <term>smṛti</term> <gloss>traditional law</gloss>. This is done in worldly activities by hunters and others. "Animal-slayer" is a Vedic form of the word. 38.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** "So many times" means the same number of counts. "Slayer of an animal in vain" means one who kills an animal not enjoined by <term>śruti</term> or <term>smṛti</term>. 38.

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** One who kills animals for his own sake without the intent of a sacrifice to the deities is a "slayer of an animal in vain." Upon death, he suffers death in birth after birth for as many times as there are hairs on the animal. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The suffix <term>kṛtvasuc</term> is used after the word "so many times" to denote the repetition of an action. Here, the word "ha" is used to indicate the notoriety of this outcome. 38.

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** He states the penalty for the opposite case: "As many as..." Here, the word "ha" denotes established tradition. 38.

( 5 ) **Nandana:** "So many times" means that many occasions. The word "ha" expresses compassion. 38.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** A person who is a slayer of an animal in vain, having committed the sin of slaughter in this world, reaches the state of becoming an animal as many times as there are hairs on the animal—eighty million hairs—in birth after birth. 38.

### Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; for the prosperity of the whole world. Therefore, slaughter in a sacrifice is not slaughter. 39.

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** This does not result in the aforementioned fault. It refers to slaughter enjoined by <term>śruti</term> and <term>smṛti</term> as part of a sacrifice, for the sake of the prosperity that arises from it. The "Self-Existent One" (Prajāpati) created or produced animals. "Himself" is an explanatory remark. "Of this world" refers to the entire universe, for which the sacrifice—such as the <term>jyotiṣṭoma</term>—is intended. "Prosperity" means wealth, sustenance, and growth. Therefore, that slaughter is to be understood as non-slaughter. This is stated because of the cessation of sin caused by violence. 39.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** Here, he removes the doubt regarding how there can be an absence of such a fault when killing for the sake of sacrifice. He says "for the sake of sacrifice." For the prosperity of the world, for its birth, because life is produced through the sequence of oblations, the sun’s nourishment, rain, and the growth of seeds leading to the production of semen. By this, it is stated that because a single animal sacrifice results in the deliverance of many living beings, such a fault does not exist. 39.

<summary>This page discusses the prohibition of killing animals for personal pleasure, advocating for the use of ghee or flour replicas in non-sacrificial contexts, and reinforces the belief that ritual animal sacrifice is exempted from the karmic consequences of violence.</summary>
<keywords>Manusmṛti, animal sacrifice, ahimsa, karmic retribution, ritual substitutes, ghee-animal</keywords>
